title: Flicker's High Flight
markdown:
In the Hanging Valleys, where the air tastes of pine and the promise of distant snow, valleys seem to float, stitched to the sky by misty veils, and streams tumble down like liquid sunlight. Nestled in a dwelling carved from a boulder the size of a sleepy bear lived Tamsin-Gob, a goblin with eyes like two bright busy magpies, always spotting the next shiny thing or interesting puzzle. Her constant shadow was Pipkin, a ferret whose every twitch and tiny chirp was a language only Tamsin-Gob truly understood. Their days were usually a gentle hum of tinkering with mountain contraptions and sharing hearth-baked root bread. But the very heart of their little world, the sparkle in their days, was Flicker.

Flicker was a puffin, and what a puffin. His beak was a splash of sunset colours, and his spirit danced as free as the mountain winds. He loved a good waddle, a daring dive, and most of all he loved to soar. His feathers, sleek black and white, gleamed in the sun. His bright curious eyes missed nothing, especially sunbeams, which he would chase with joyful abandon, leaving small delightful messes in his wake.

Higher and higher went Flicker, whenever the sky said please.

“Pipkin,” Tamsin-Gob said one sun-drenched morning, her voice a soft flustered sound that was unusual for her. “Pipkin, have you seen Flicker? He is not in his nest, and he is not by the sun-dial.”

Pipkin, who had been polishing a tiny brass cog with a piece of moss, froze. His little nose twitched, sampling the air. He looked towards the open doorway, where sunlight streamed in like a golden invitation, and then he looked up, bright eyes wide.

And there, against the vast impossibly blue canvas of the sky, was Flicker. A small dark speck, rising, rising, rising on invisible currents. He was not just flying. He was exploring. Higher and higher went Flicker, a tiny white flash against the deep azure.

A tremor shook Tamsin-Gob’s shoulders. Her hands flew to her mouth. This was no lost slipper or misplaced tool. This was her Flicker, her mischievous beloved Flicker, heading for the very roof of the world. He was so small, and the sky so immense. “Oh, Flicker,” she whispered, a wobble in her voice.

Pipkin darted forward, a blur of brown fur. He nudged Tamsin-Gob’s hand with his soft nose, then chirped urgently, his body language a clear message: we go, we get him. His confidence was a small but powerful anchor.

And so they set out. Tamsin-Gob, trusty walking staff in hand, followed Pipkin onto the winding mountain path. It was a dappled track where pine shadows lay striped across the ancient stone, the air growing cooler as they ascended. The wind whispered secrets through the gnarled branches of fir trees that leaned as if in greeting, needles rustling like tiny applause. Pipkin scampered ahead, keen eyes scanning the way, tail a vibrant question mark.

They rounded a bend that opened onto a breathtaking vista of the lower valleys, and there, perched precariously on a ledge that looked as if it had been chipped from the sky itself, was Grumble-Snout. His mobile trading post, a sturdy brightly painted cart pulled by a remarkably patient shaggy mountain yak, overflowed with a bewildering assortment of items. He greeted them with a grin that showed off his surprisingly clean teeth, and a voice that had the gravelly warmth of a rumbling avalanche.

“Tamsin-Gob. Pipkin. A fine day for an expedition, wouldn’t you say?” he boomed, tipping a cap adorned with a colourful feather. “Out for a bit of mountain exploration, are we?”

Tamsin-Gob, trying to keep her voice steady, explained. “Grumble-Snout, have you by any chance seen a puffin flying very, very high? Much higher than usual?”

Grumble-Snout stroked his chin, eyes twinkling with a mixture of concern and opportunity. “A puffin, you say? High? Well, I might have just the thing.” He rummaged enthusiastically in his cart, elbows bumping against various jars and trinkets. He produced a large intricately woven net made of what looked like spun moonlight. “Behold,” he declared, unfurling it with a flourish. “The Sky-Fisher’s Delight. Perfect for snagging creatures from the ether, right out of the blue.”

Tamsin-Gob stared at the net. It was beautifully made, no doubt, but Flicker was not a fish. He was her pet, her feathered friend. “That is very kind, Grumble-Snout,” she said politely. “But I do not think Flicker is one for fishing, even from the sky.”

“Ah, right you are.” Grumble-Snout chuckled, tucking the net away with surprising speed. “A discerning creature, I am sure. Perhaps something else then.” He rummaged again, this time producing a long slender pole topped with a polished crystal. “The Cloud-Walker’s Staff. Guaranteed to keep your feet dry, even when traversing the fluffiest cumulus. You will never get a soggy sock again.”

Tamsin-Gob’s shoulders slumped. A walking stick for clouds was of absolutely no use when Flicker was miles above the nearest wisp of vapour, a tiny speck against the overwhelming blue. Just as despair began to settle in her chest like a heavy stone, a sound, faint but unmistakable, echoed down from the peaks. Honk. Honk.

It was Flicker.

“He is up there,” Tamsin-Gob cried, pointing with a trembling finger towards the highest, most ancient-looking pine tree she had ever seen. It stood sentinel against the sky, its trunk as wide as a small house, its branches reaching like wizened fingers towards the heavens. And there, perched on its very topmost twig, a mere needle point against the vastness, was Flicker. He looked remarkably unconcerned, a tiny statue surveying the world spread out below him like a rumpled green and brown blanket.

They scrambled upwards, the pine shadows stretching and shrinking like playful spirits as the sun climbed higher. Tamsin-Gob called Flicker’s name, her voice carried away by the brisk mountain breeze. She cooed and whistled, mimicking his favourite playful sounds, offering imaginary treats. But Flicker, though he watched her, seemed utterly content in his lofty perch. He was not stuck, not truly. He was simply enjoying the view. He tilted his head, his beak catching the sunlight, as if contemplating the sheer scale of it all.

Higher and higher went Flicker — until going higher was only looking.

Pipkin, ever observant, darted around the base of the great pine, nose to the ground. He nudged a loose coil of something grey and springy with his paw. Tamsin-Gob recognised it instantly. It was a length of liquorice rope, strong and sweet-smelling, that Grumble-Snout often sold for building goblin kites and making sturdy chewable toys.

A brilliant idea sparked. Flicker loved soaring. He loved seeing the world from a new perspective. But he also loved her, and he loved treats. He was not trying to escape. He was trying to see.

Grumble-Snout, as if summoned by the very thought of a trade, reappeared, his yak patiently chewing its cud. “Trouble, Tamsin-Gob?” he asked, pulling a small brass whistle from his pouch. “I have just the thing. This will call any bird, guaranteed. It is tuned to the frequency of… well, something bird-like, at any rate.”

Tamsin-Gob smiled, a genuine warm smile that reached her bright curious eyes. “Grumble-Snout,” she said, voice clear and steady, carrying a new confidence. “I think I have just what Flicker needs. And I think I know how to get him down safely.”

She took the liquorice rope. She did not try to climb the impossibly tall tree. Instead she looped the rope, creating a sturdy wide cradle that swayed gently in the breeze. Then she reached into her satchel and pulled out a truly magnificent glistening mountain berry — plump, crimson, and bursting with sweet juice. It was one of Flicker’s absolute favourites. She dangled it just within reach of his beak, where it sparkled enticingly.

Flicker eyed the berry. He eyed the liquorice rope-swing, which looked strangely like a new kind of perch. He eyed Tamsin-Gob, his familiar loving goblin, who was offering him not just a treat, but a ride. He gave a happy honk and, with a little hop, landed not on the ground, but squarely in the liquorice cradle.

With Pipkin holding one end of the rope steady, his small body braced against a thick root, Tamsin-Gob gently, carefully, lowered Flicker. The liquorice rope swayed just enough to feel like a thrilling descent, a controlled flight. The berry remained tantalisingly close. The wind whistled a cheerful tune around them.

Back on the ground, Flicker waddled into Tamsin-Gob’s waiting arms, nuzzling her cheek with his beak, letting out a series of contented chirps. The adventure had been thrilling for him, a grand exploration of the skies. For Tamsin-Gob, it had been a lesson in understanding his curious spirit, and she kept that lesson in her hands rather than in a speech.

That evening, back in their home, Tamsin-Gob built Flicker a new perch. It was higher than any branch in their garden, a specially crafted platform that allowed him to gaze at the sky, the distant peaks, and the swirling mists, just as he loved to do. But it was also safe, secure, and close to home, where his favourite goblin and ferret friends waited.

Flicker honked his happy approval, snuggled close to Tamsin-Gob, a contented puffin with a newfound appreciation for safe heights. Pipkin made a rumbling sound of pure contentment, curled up on Tamsin-Gob’s lap. Higher and higher went Flicker — and home was still the highest place that knew his name.
characters: Tamsin-Gob (goblin with magpie-bright eyes), Pipkin (a ferret who speaks in twitches), Flicker (a puffin who loves to soar)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
